title: Brent Crude Is Up 85% Since January. OXY, XOM, and CVX Are Playing It Very Differently. - AOL.com
content: Oil prices have risen dramatically in 2026, driven higher by the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East. Some of the most important oil companies didn't benefit as much as you would expect because of regional exposure, timing, and hedging activity. 10 stocks we like better than Occidental Petroleum › Occidental Petroleum (NYSE: OXY) beat Wall Street estimates by a wide margin when it reported first-quarter 2026 earnings. Analysts were expecting earnings of $0.59 per share, but the company reported $1.06 per share. That's an impressive beat, but management admits that it could have done better. What's going on with the company and with peers like Chevron (NYSE: CVX) and ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM)? One of the first big problems in the quarter for oil companies was the timing of the oil price spike. Most of the advance occurred after the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East began, so the spike that has pushed oil prices up 85% in 2026 as of this writing didn't really get underway until March. So, energy companies only benefited from higher oil prices for a short period. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » This is why analyst expectations for the second quarter are much higher than expectations for the first quarter. For example, Wall Street is projecting Oxy to earn $1.58 per share in the second quarter. But another issue hampered Oxy's performance in the first quarter: hedging. Oil companies routinely hedge their production to protect against price movements in energy markets. In this case, that hedging turned into a headwind. Oxy, which is much less exposed to the Middle East than Exxon or Chevron, was a relative standout. At the other extreme was Exxon, which has more exposure to the region and saw its production impacted. That said, its $1.16 per share in earnings beat the analyst call of $1.01. But hedging led to a $700 million earnings hit. That should be reversed in the second quarter as shipments hedged are delivered. Still, the short-term impact is worth noting as you examine the business. Chevron, meanwhile, fell between Exxon and Oxy, with its $1.41 per share earnings beating Wall Street's $0.97 per share call. But once again, the company's hedging activity was a headwind, as management took a $2.9 billion charge related to it. Hedging is company-specific, with each company adopting a different approach. And because hedging is a proprietary activity, investors won't know about the impact, good or bad, until the company releases quarterly results. That said, the refining operations of Exxon and Chevron performed weakly, with timing and hedging both playing a role. Oxy recently sold its downstream business at the start of 2026, so this business wasn't a meaningful issue for the company in the quarter. Simply put, there are a lot of moving parts to consider when you look at individual energy companies. In the end, Oxy, Exxon, and Chevron are all benefiting from rising energy prices, but the way they are playing the rise is slightly different. And that, in turn, is leading to different outcomes. title: Is Exxon Mobil's Recent Surge Sustainable Amid Middle East Tensions - Kavout
content: Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock has been a standout performer in recent weeks, with shares trading at $154.19 as of March 2, 2026, up 1.11% on the day and nearing its 52-week high of $159.35. This impressive run, which saw the stock climb from $115.15 on November 30, 2025, to $152.50 by March 1, 2026—a 32.4% increase—is largely attributed to a dramatic shift in the global energy landscape. The "Midnight Hammer" crisis in the Middle East, characterized by retaliatory strikes and a de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has injected a significant risk premium into crude oil markets. This geopolitical shock has sent oil prices soaring, with WTI crude currently at $71.15 per barrel, having recently spiked towards $73 and Brent crude briefly touching $100 per barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for 20% of global seaborne oil, has seen shipping halted and war risk coverage cancelled by marine insurers, effectively stranding an estimated 15 million barrels per day (bpd) of global supply. This immediate supply disruption, combined with a perceived failure of OPEC+ to adequately increase production, has fueled a rapid "risk-off" rotation into hard assets like oil. The market's reaction on March 2, 2026, saw XOM and Occidental Petroleum (OXY) both climb 2.1% by midday, even as the broader S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite tumbled. This divergence underscores a fundamental reassessment of value in an uncertain geopolitical climate, where the "old economy" energy trade has become a defensive hedge. While the immediate catalyst is conflict, the underlying "AI Power Crunch"—the insatiable demand for energy to fuel massive data centers—is also contributing to a structural revaluation of energy companies. However, the sustainability of this surge hinges precariously on the resolution of the Strait of Hormuz standoff. Analysts warn that a diplomatic "off-ramp" within the next 72 hours could lead to a significant cooling of oil prices. Conversely, if the blockade persists, a "super-spike" toward $120 per barrel is possible, which would almost certainly tip the broader global economy into a recession by Q3 2026. This delicate balance means XOM's recent gains, while substantial, are tied to highly unpredictable global events. The current surge in oil prices provides a significant tailwind for Exxon Mobil's Q1 2026 earnings, potentially rewriting near-term cash flow math. Higher crude prices directly enhance the profitability of Exxon's Upstream segment, which saw a 41% increase in revenue in Q1 2025, including a remarkable 234% jump in its U.S. Upstream operations. This segment is particularly sensitive to commodity price fluctuations, making the current environment highly favorable for top-line growth and margin expansion. Despite a 6% decline in net profit and a 15% fall in EPS in Q1 2025 due to weaker refining margins and petrochemicals, the company demonstrated resilience later in the year. Exxon Mobil reported strong Q3 2025 earnings of $7.5 billion and $14.8 billion in cash flow, followed by a Q4 2025 EPS of $1.71, beating estimates. This consistent outperformance, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of earnings beats, suggests an underlying operational strength that can capitalize on improved market conditions. Analysts are already adjusting their expectations, with Bank of America raising ExxonMobil's price target from $135 to $151, reflecting confidence in enhanced future profitability due to the oil risk premium. The consensus Q1 2026 EPS is projected at approximately $1.53, a figure that could prove conservative if oil prices remain elevated throughout the quarter. Exxon's ability to generate substantial free cash flow, projected at $52 billion for the 2025-2026 period, further strengthens its financial position to navigate market dynamics. However, it's not a clear-cut picture. While Upstream benefits, the Energy Products (refining) and Chemical Products segments can face margin pressures. In Q1 2025, Energy Products revenue declined 4% and Chemical Products revenue fell 8%, largely due to falling refining margins and an oversupply in the global chemical market. Therefore, while high crude prices boost one side of the business, investors must monitor product solutions segment margins and overall production guidance during the Q1 2026 earnings call, expected in late April, to gauge the full impact. Beyond the immediate tailwinds from geopolitical tensions, Exxon Mobil's long-term investment thesis is underpinned by its strategic focus on "advantaged barrels" and robust production growth from key assets. The company's operations in Guyana, particularly the Stabroek block, are a cornerstone of this strategy. Projects like Uaru, expected to start up by year-end 2026 with a capacity of 250,000 b/d, and Whiptail, forecast to add another 250,000 b/d next year, are set to boost Guyana's daily oil production well beyond 1 million b/d. Exxon Mobil is also actively developing Guyana's significant recoverable gas resources, especially in the southeast part of the Stabroek block. The Hammerhead project, for instance, is designed to transport gas by pipeline to shore, complementing oil production. The company has already completed its first gas-to-energy pipeline, awaiting an onshore power plant to lower electricity costs in Guyana. This integrated approach to resource development highlights Exxon's commitment to maximizing value from its world-class geology and competitive development costs. The Permian Basin in the U.S. shale patch remains another critical growth engine. CEO Darren Woods has stated there is "no near-term peak Permian" for Exxon, citing over 40 technologies currently in testing to enhance recovery and efficiency. This focus on low-cost, high-margin production in both Guyana and the Permian has made XOM a "HALO" stock (Heavy-Asset, Low Obsolescence) for investors seeking stability and long-term value. Furthermore, Exxon Mobil's commitment to shareholder returns is a significant draw. The company has a strong track record of distributing capital through dividends and share repurchases, having distributed $9.4 billion in Q3 2025 and $9.5 billion in Q4 2025. As a dividend Aristocrat, boasting 26 consecutive annual dividend increases, XOM offers a compelling proposition for income-focused investors, signaling management's confidence in its ability to generate sustained free cash flow and maintain financial discipline. While Exxon Mobil benefits from current market dynamics, several significant risks could derail its long-term investment thesis. The most immediate concern remains commodity price volatility. Despite recent spikes, energy prices are inherently sensitive to geopolitical events, OPEC+ decisions, and global demand fluctuations. A sharp decline in prices, whether due to de-escalation in the Middle East, falling global demand, or oversupply, could significantly reduce ExxonMobil’s income, particularly in its highly profitable Upstream segment. Beyond oil prices, the company faces regulatory and political risks. Stricter environmental legislation globally, including potential bans on exploration in sensitive regions, new emissions standards, and tighter regulation of refining, could increase operating costs or limit production capacity. The accelerating global energy transition to lower-carbon sources poses a fundamental threat to long-term demand for fossil fuels, potentially diminishing Exxon Mobil's core product revenue streams and creating significant market risks. Exxon Mobil's diversified earnings are also susceptible to global chemical market oversupply and weak refining margins. As seen in Q1 2025, the chemical segment experienced substantial earnings reductions due to "bottom-of-cycle" margins. This cyclicality can act as a significant drag, even when other segments perform well. The capital-intensive nature of its upstream and downstream mix constrains revenue growth assumptions, keeping them modest at around 2.3%. Finally, valuation concerns persist among some analysts. title: Is ExxonMobil's Guyana Expansion a Game-Changer for XOM Stock - Kavout
content: ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM) is at a pivotal juncture with its ambitious offshore development plans in Guyana, particularly as it navigates the environmental approval process for the Longtail and Haimara projects. The company's recent submission of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for Longtail and the subsequent public consultations, which began on April 13, 2026, mark a crucial step toward unlocking significant future production. This move is not merely procedural; it represents a strategic doubling down on one of the world's most promising new oil frontiers, potentially reshaping XOM's long-term growth trajectory and shareholder value. However, the path is fraught with environmental and regulatory challenges that demand careful consideration from investors. The proposed Longtail development, ExxonMobil's eighth in the Stabroek Block, is projected to begin production in 2030 and operate for approximately 30 years. This long-term horizon underscores the strategic importance of Guyana to ExxonMobil's portfolio, especially given the project's substantial output estimates of 1.2 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day and around 250,000 barrels per day of condensate. With XOM currently trading at $154.92 as of May 22, 2026, and a market capitalization of $642.14 billion, the successful sanctioning and development of these projects are essential to fuel future earnings growth, particularly against a backdrop of -4.5% year-over-year revenue decline in FY2025. The ongoing public consultations, led by ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge, aim to address community concerns and integrate feedback into the EIA process, a critical component for securing final authorization from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The Longtail and Haimara projects are cornerstones of ExxonMobil's aggressive expansion strategy in Guyana's Stabroek Block, a prolific offshore basin that has yielded numerous world-class discoveries. ExxonMobil operates the Stabroek Block with a 45% interest, alongside partners Hess (now owned by Chevron) with 30% and CNOOC with 25%. This consortium has transformed Guyana into a major global oil producer in a remarkably short period, with Longtail representing the eighth and Haimara the expected ninth development within this block. The sheer scale of these developments is staggering; Longtail alone is designed to produce 250,000 barrels per day of condensate and 1.2 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas, contributing significantly to global energy supply for decades. These projects are strategically located in what ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge refers to as the "southeast gas area" of the Stabroek Block. Longtail is positioned as the anchor for several discoveries in its vicinity, while Haimara is slated to anchor the subsequent project. The company submitted the Field Development Plan (FDP) for Longtail by the end of March 2026, signaling its readiness to move forward once environmental authorizations are secured. The projected start of production in 2030 for Longtail, with an operational lifespan of roughly 30 years, provides a clear long-term revenue stream for ExxonMobil, bolstering its upstream segment and providing a hedge against potential declines in mature assets elsewhere. For ExxonMobil, these developments are crucial for maintaining its production profile and driving future cash flow, especially as the company navigates a dynamic global energy landscape. The Stabroek Block discoveries have been instrumental in XOM's recent performance, and continued success here is vital for offsetting the -23.1% year-over-year decline in free cash flow observed in FY2025. The consistent stream of new projects, each requiring substantial capital investment but promising high returns, underpins the company's commitment to its fossil fuel portfolio while also acknowledging the increasing demand for natural gas as a transition fuel. The successful execution of Longtail and Haimara will solidify Guyana's role as a core growth engine for ExxonMobil for the foreseeable future. The successful development of the Longtail and Haimara projects in Guyana holds profound implications for ExxonMobil's financial outlook, promising to inject substantial revenue and cash flow into the company's operations starting in 2030. With Longtail alone projected to add 250,000 barrels per day of condensate and 1.2 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas, these volumes represent a significant boost to XOM's overall production capacity. This increased output is critical for a company that saw its revenue decline by -4.5% year-over-year in FY2025 and net income fall by -14.4% during the same period. The new production streams are expected to reverse these trends, providing a much-needed catalyst for top-line and bottom-line growth. From a valuation perspective, ExxonMobil currently trades at a P/E ratio of 25.60, which is relatively high for an integrated oil major, suggesting that investors are already anticipating future growth from projects like those in Guyana. The company's TTM EPS stands at $6.05, and the expected production from Longtail, operating for 30 years, will contribute significantly to future earnings per share. While the immediate impact on financials is still several years away, the certainty of these projects moving forward, contingent on environmental approvals, provides a strong long-term investment thesis. The company's dividend yield of 2.6%, with a payout ratio of 68.1%, is supported by its robust cash generation, which these new projects are designed to enhance further. Moreover, the sheer scale of the Stabroek Block's reserves and the continuous stream of new developments offer a long runway for capital allocation and shareholder returns. The $642.14 billion market cap reflects ExxonMobil's dominant position, but sustained growth requires consistent project execution. The Longtail project's contribution to free cash flow, which saw a -23.1% decline in FY2025, will be vital for improving financial flexibility, funding future exploration, and potentially increasing shareholder distributions. The company's relatively low debt-to-equity ratio of 0.19 and a net debt-to-EBITDA of 0.65 provide ample capacity to finance these large-scale developments, underscoring a disciplined financial approach even as it pursues aggressive growth in Guyana. ExxonMobil's ambitious development plans in Guyana, while promising significant returns, are not without substantial environmental and regulatory hurdles. The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process for the Longtail project, which commenced public consultations on April 13, 2026, is a critical phase that requires addressing concerns from local communities and environmental advocates. ExxonMobil Guyana President Alistair Routledge emphasized the importance of these 60-day consultations, stating they are designed to allow residents to review studies and raise concerns, ensuring risks are mitigated. However, past experiences suggest that public engagement in Guyana's EIA process has been limited, with a lack of public awareness and understanding often leading to insufficient feedback, as highlighted in a critical review of the process. A major point of contention revolves around oil spill liability. A June 2023 decision by an appeals court ordered ExxonMobil to put up $2 billion for Guyana oil spill costs, but critically, it shifted the remaining uncapped liability onto the Guyanese people. This decision, which followed a lower court ruling that had initially held ExxonMobil fully responsible, has been widely criticized by organizations like the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) for exposing Guyana to significant financial risk. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill, which cost BP and its insurers $70 billion, serves as a stark reminder of the potential scale of such disasters, far exceeding the $2 billion bond. This lack of full financial assurance from ExxonMobil's parent company remains a significant environmental and reputational risk. Furthermore, the legal framework governing oil and gas in Guyana has been described as evolving. The Environmental Protection Act of 1996, initially lacked specific guidelines for the oil and gas sector, which only emerged as a major industry after ExxonMobil's Liza-1 discovery in May 2015. While the EPA now requires EIAs for projects like Longtail, concerns persist about the sufficiency of consultation periods and the adequacy of addressing social and cultural issues. The company's own Oil Spill Response Plan for Guyana Operations, last revised in December 2025, outlines safeguards, but the ongoing debate about liability and transparency, particularly regarding the actual terms and scope of insurance coverage, continues to cast a shadow over ExxonMobil's operations in the region. Guyana has rapidly become an indispensable pillar of ExxonMobil's global strategy, representing one of the most significant growth engines for the energy giant. The Stabroek Block discoveries, initiated with Liza-1 in 2015, have transformed the country into a crucial source of future production, particularly as the company navigates a complex energy transition and seeks to maintain its competitive edge. With an operational interest of 45% in the Stabroek Block, ExxonMobil is heavily invested in unlocking the vast hydrocarbon potential of this region, which is expected to underpin its upstream segment for decades. The Longtail and Haimara projects, slated for production starting in 2030 and operating for 30 years, are central to this long-term vision. The strategic importance of Guyana is amplified by its role in diversifying ExxonMobil's asset base and providing high-margin barrels. Unlike some mature fields that face declining production and higher operating costs, Guyana offers prolific, low-cost production that enhances XOM's overall profitability and resilience. This focus on high-quality, advantaged assets is a core tenet of CEO Darren W. Woods' strategy, aiming to improve capital efficiency and shareholder returns. The projected output of 250,000 barrels per day from Longtail alone, combined with substantial natural gas volumes, will contribute significantly to ExxonMobil's global production targets and cash flow generation, which is crucial given the -5.5% decline in operating cash flow in FY2025. Moreover, Guyana's emergence as a major oil producer reshapes regional energy security and offers a stable, democratic partner for the U.S. in South America. In both resources, the breakeven costs are low. With its solid portfolio of upstream assets, COP is well-positioned to gain. The upstream energy giant has low-cost drilling opportunities across Permian, Eagle Ford and Bakken that could be successfully developed over two decades.
